procedure: At the branch the patient gives their referral ID at the front desk and pays.
A trained phlebotomist cleans the inside of the elbow and draws a small amount of blood from a vein with a sterile needle.
A plaster is put on the spot; the patient can go home or back to work straight away.
blood.preparation: No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.

procedure: At the branch the patient gives their referral ID at the front desk and pays.
The lab confirms the patient has fasted.
A small amount of blood is drawn from a vein in the arm with a sterile needle.
A plaster is put on the spot; the patient can eat and drink straight after.
bloodFasting.preparation: Fast for 8–12 hours before the test — no food or drinks except plain water. Coming early in the morning makes fasting easier.

fingerPrick.sample: Blood drop (finger prick) or blood sample
procedure: At the branch the patient gives their referral ID at the front desk and pays.
The fingertip is cleaned and pricked with a small sterile lancet (or blood is drawn from the arm).
A drop of blood is collected and tested.
At the branch the patient gives their referral ID at the front desk and pays.
The patient is given a sterile container and shown to a private toilet.
After cleaning the genital area, the patient passes the first bit of urine into the toilet, then collects the middle part of the stream ("midstream") in the container.
The closed container is handed to the lab.
urine.preparation: If possible, give the first urine of the morning. Women should tell staff if they are on their period.

procedure: The patient collects a large container from the branch.
On day 1 the first morning urine is passed into the toilet; every drop of urine after that, for 24 hours, goes into the container (kept cool).
The next morning the first urine is added and the container is brought back to the branch.
urine24.preparation: Collect the container first and follow the written instructions exactly — missing any urine affects the result.
urine24.duration: 24 hours of collection at home; a few minutes to drop it off

procedure: At the branch the patient gives their referral ID at the front desk and pays.
The patient is given a clean container with a small scoop.
A small amount of stool is collected (not mixed with urine or water) and the container is closed.
The sample is handed to the lab — ideally within 1–2 hours of collection.
stool.preparation: Collect the container from the branch first. Tell the lab about any antibiotics or diarrhoea medicine being taken.
stool.duration: A few minutes to hand in

procedure: At the branch the patient gives their referral ID at the front desk and pays.
A health worker gently rubs a sterile cotton swab over the area (throat, ear, wound or skin).
The swab goes into a sealed tube and is sent to the lab to grow and identify any germs.
swab.preparation: If possible, come before starting antibiotics. For a throat swab, don’t eat or drink for 30 minutes before.

procedure: At the branch the patient gives their referral ID at the front desk and pays.
The test is done in a private room, with a chaperone if the patient wishes.
For women a speculum is gently inserted and a soft swab is taken from the vagina or cervix; for men a thin swab is taken from the opening of the urethra.
The swab goes into a sealed tube for the lab.
genitalSwab.preparation: Avoid sex, douching and vaginal creams for 24–48 hours before. Not during a heavy period. Men should not urinate for about 1 hour before a urethral swab.

procedure: The patient is given a sterile container.
The sample is produced by masturbation into the container in a private room at the branch (or at home, if the lab allows).
A home sample must reach the lab within 1 hour, kept at body temperature (e.g. in an inside pocket).
semen.preparation: No ejaculation for 2–5 days before the test (but not more than 7). Avoid alcohol for a few days. Do not use lubricants or condoms to collect the sample.

procedure: Early in the morning the patient rinses the mouth with plain water (no toothpaste).
The patient takes a few deep breaths and coughs deeply to bring up phlegm from the chest — not saliva — into a sterile container.
The container is closed and brought to the lab. Some tests need samples on 3 days in a row.
sputum.preparation: Collect the container from the branch first. The early-morning sample is the best one.

procedure: The fluid is collected by a doctor in hospital through a lumbar puncture (a thin needle in the lower back under local anaesthetic).
The sample is brought to the lab quickly for testing.
csf.preparation: Arranged by the patient’s doctor or hospital — the branch receives and tests the sample.

procedure: At the branch the patient gives their referral ID at the front desk and pays.
The patient breathes into a small bag or tube to give a first breath sample.
The patient drinks a special solution, then waits about 15–30 minutes.
A second breath sample is taken and the two are compared.
breath.preparation: Fast for at least 6 hours. Stop antibiotics 4 weeks and stomach-acid medicines (e.g. omeprazole) 2 weeks before, if the doctor agrees.

procedure: A doctor removes a small piece of tissue during a biopsy or surgery.
The tissue is placed in a preservative and sent to the lab.
Thin slices are prepared and examined under the microscope by a pathologist.
tissue.preparation: The sample is taken by the patient’s doctor; the patient usually does not need to come to the branch for this test.

procedure: At the branch the patient gives their referral ID at the front desk and pays.
The skin over the lump is cleaned.
A very thin needle is passed into the lump and a few cells are drawn into a syringe (sometimes guided by ultrasound).
Light pressure is applied and a small plaster put on; the cells are examined under the microscope.
fnac.preparation: Usually no preparation. Tell staff about blood-thinning medicines.

procedure: At the branch the patient gives their referral ID at the front desk and pays.
In a private room the patient lies on a couch; a speculum is gently inserted into the vagina.
A small soft brush is used to collect cells from the cervix (neck of the womb).
The cells are sent to the lab. It may be slightly uncomfortable but is quick.
cervical.preparation: Best done mid-cycle, not during a period. Avoid sex, douching and vaginal creams for 48 hours before.

procedure: At the branch the patient gives their referral ID at the front desk and pays.
The patient removes jewellery and metal items and may change into a gown.
The radiographer positions the body part between the X-ray machine and the detector — often from two angles (front and side).
The patient keeps very still (and may hold the breath) for a few seconds while each picture is taken. It is painless.
xray.preparation: No special preparation. Remove metal items around the area. Tell staff if the patient is or may be pregnant.

procedure: At the branch the patient gives their referral ID at the front desk and pays.
The patient changes into a gown.
The patient drinks (or, for an enema, is given through the back passage) a white barium liquid that shows up on X-ray.
The radiologist takes moving and still X-ray pictures as the barium passes through, sometimes asking the patient to turn on the table.
Afterwards the patient drinks plenty of water; stools may be pale for a day or two.
xrayBarium.preparation: Usually no food or drink for 6 hours before. A barium enema needs bowel preparation (laxatives) the day before — the branch gives the instructions.
xrayBarium.duration: About 30–60 minutes (follow-through can take a few hours)

procedure: At the branch the patient gives their referral ID at the front desk and pays.
The patient changes into a gown and lies on the X-ray table.
A contrast dye is gently put into the area being studied (through a thin tube or catheter).
X-ray pictures are taken as the dye fills the area; the tube is then removed.
xrayContrast.preparation: The branch gives specific instructions when booking. Tell staff about allergies to contrast dye and about pregnancy.

hsg.sample: X-ray of the womb and tubes with contrast dye
procedure: At the branch the patient gives their referral ID at the front desk and pays.
The patient lies on the X-ray table as for a smear test; a speculum is inserted.
A thin tube is passed through the cervix and a contrast dye is gently put into the womb.
X-ray pictures show the dye filling the womb and flowing through the fallopian tubes. Cramping like period pain is common for a short time.
hsg.preparation: Booked between day 7 and day 10 of the cycle (after the period ends, before ovulation). Avoid unprotected sex from the period until the test. A painkiller 30–60 minutes before can help.

procedure: At the branch the patient gives their referral ID at the front desk and pays.
The patient undresses to the waist in private.
Each breast in turn is placed on the machine and gently pressed between two plates for a few seconds while the picture is taken — usually two views of each breast.
It can be uncomfortable for a few seconds but is quick.
mammogram.preparation: Do not use deodorant, talcum powder or lotion under the arms or on the breasts on the day. Best done the week after a period, when breasts are less tender.

procedure: At the branch the patient gives their referral ID at the front desk and pays.
The patient completes a safety checklist and removes all metal (jewellery, watch, hairpins, phone, cards) and changes into a gown.
The patient lies on a table that slides into the tunnel-shaped scanner; the part being scanned is placed in a padded coil.
The scanner makes loud knocking sounds — earplugs or headphones are given. The patient must keep very still; the radiographer talks through an intercom.
Some scans need a contrast injection into a vein half-way through.
mri.preparation: Remove all metal. Tell staff before booking about a pacemaker, metal implants, clips, shrapnel, pregnancy, kidney problems or fear of closed spaces. Some abdominal scans need 4–6 hours of fasting.

procedure: At the branch the patient gives their referral ID at the front desk and pays.
The patient lies on a couch and uncovers the area being scanned.
A cool gel is put on the skin and a small handheld probe is moved over it; sound waves make live pictures on a screen.
It is painless and uses no radiation. The gel is wiped off afterwards.
ultrasound.preparation: No special preparation. Wear loose, comfortable clothing.

procedure: At the branch the patient gives their referral ID at the front desk and pays.
The patient lies on a couch and uncovers the tummy.
A cool gel is put on the skin and a small probe is moved over the abdomen to see the organs on a screen.
It is painless and uses no radiation.
ultrasoundFasting.preparation: No food for 6–8 hours before (plain water is fine), so the gallbladder and organs show clearly. For the pelvic part, drink 4–6 glasses of water an hour before and don’t empty the bladder.

procedure: At the branch the patient gives their referral ID at the front desk and pays.
The patient lies on a couch and uncovers the lower tummy.
Gel is put on the skin and a small probe is moved over the lower abdomen; a full bladder helps the organs behind it show clearly.
It is painless and uses no radiation. The patient can empty the bladder afterwards.
ultrasoundBladder.preparation: Come with a full bladder: drink 4–6 glasses (about 1 litre) of water an hour before and do not urinate until after the scan.

procedure: At the branch the patient gives their referral ID at the front desk and pays.
In a private room (a chaperone can be present) the patient empties the bladder and lies on the couch.
A slim probe with a protective cover and gel is gently placed a little way into the vagina; it gives clearer pictures of the womb and ovaries.
It may feel like pressure but should not hurt.
ultrasoundTransvaginal.preparation: Empty the bladder just before the scan. It can be done during a period.

procedure: At the branch the patient gives their referral ID at the front desk and pays.
In a private room the patient lies on the left side with knees bent.
A lubricated probe, about the width of a finger, is gently placed into the back passage to view the prostate.
It may feel like pressure; it takes only a few minutes.
ultrasoundTransrectal.preparation: An enema or bowel emptying may be asked for before the scan; the branch gives instructions. A partly full bladder may be needed.

ultrasoundInfant.sample: Ultrasound images of a baby’s brain
procedure: At the branch the patient gives their referral ID at the front desk and pays.
The baby lies on the couch or a parent’s lap.
Gel is put on the soft spot (fontanelle) on top of the head and a small probe is moved gently over it to see the brain.
It is painless and uses no radiation.
ultrasoundInfant.preparation: Feed the baby shortly before so they are calm or asleep. Only possible while the soft spot is still open (usually under 12–18 months).

procedure: At the branch the patient gives their referral ID at the front desk and pays.
The patient lies on a couch and uncovers the area (legs, neck, abdomen or other).
Gel is put on the skin and the probe is moved along the blood vessels; the machine shows and sounds the blood flow.
It is painless and uses no radiation.
doppler.preparation: No special preparation. Wear loose clothing.

procedure: At the branch the patient gives their referral ID at the front desk and pays.
The patient removes metal items and may change into a gown.
The patient lies on a table that moves slowly through a large ring-shaped scanner.
The patient keeps still and follows breathing instructions; the scan itself takes only a few minutes and is painless.
ct.preparation: Remove metal items. Tell staff if the patient is or may be pregnant.

procedure: At the branch the patient gives their referral ID at the front desk and pays.
Staff check kidney function and allergies; a small cannula is placed in an arm vein. For abdominal scans the patient may drink a contrast liquid first.
The patient lies on a table that moves through a ring-shaped scanner; contrast dye is injected — it can cause a warm feeling or a metallic taste for a moment.
After the scan the patient waits a short time and drinks plenty of water to flush the dye out.
ctContrast.preparation: No food for 4–6 hours before (water is fine). Tell staff about allergies to contrast or iodine, kidney disease, diabetes medicine (metformin) and pregnancy. A recent kidney test (E/U/C) may be requested.

colonoscopy.sample: Camera examination of the large bowel
procedure: At the branch the patient gives their referral ID at the front desk and pays.
The patient changes into a gown; a sedative may be given to relax them.
Lying on the left side, a thin flexible tube with a camera is passed through the back passage to look at the whole large bowel.
Small samples (biopsies) or polyps may be removed painlessly. The patient rests until the sedation wears off.
colonoscopy.preparation: The bowel must be empty: a low-fibre diet for 2 days, clear fluids only the day before and a bowel-cleansing laxative as instructed by the branch. If sedated, someone must accompany the patient home.

upperEndoscopy.sample: Camera examination of the gullet and stomach
procedure: At the branch the patient gives their referral ID at the front desk and pays.
The throat is numbed with a spray and/or a sedative is given.
A mouth guard is placed and a thin flexible tube with a camera is passed through the mouth into the gullet, stomach and first part of the bowel.
Small samples can be taken painlessly. The patient rests briefly afterwards and should not eat until the throat feels normal.
upperEndoscopy.preparation: No food for 6–8 hours and no drinks for 2–4 hours before. If sedated, someone must accompany the patient home.

procedure: At the branch the patient gives their referral ID at the front desk and pays.
The nose and throat may be numbed with a spray.
A thin, flexible camera is passed gently through the nose (or a mirror/scope through the mouth) to look at the throat and voice box.
The patient may be asked to speak or swallow during the test.
pharyngoscopy.preparation: Usually avoid eating for 2 hours before; the branch confirms.

procedure: At the branch the patient gives their referral ID at the front desk and pays.
The patient lies down and uncovers the chest, wrists and ankles.
Small sticky pads (electrodes) are placed on the chest, arms and legs and connected to the ECG machine.
The patient lies still and breathes normally for a few minutes while the heart’s electrical activity is recorded. It is painless.
ecg.preparation: Avoid body lotion or oil on the chest on the day. Wear a top that is easy to remove. Bring a list of medicines.

procedure: At the branch the patient gives their referral ID at the front desk and pays.
Sticky pads are placed on the chest and connected to a small recorder worn on a belt or strap.
The patient goes home and carries on with normal daily life for 24 hours, writing down any symptoms and the time they happen.
The patient returns the next day to have the recorder removed; the recording is analysed.
holter.preparation: Have a bath or shower before coming — the recorder must not get wet. Wear loose clothing. Avoid electric blankets and keep phones a little away from the recorder.
holter.duration: About 15 minutes to fit, then 24 hours at home

procedure: At the branch the patient gives their referral ID at the front desk and pays.
The patient undresses to the waist and lies on the left side on a couch.
ECG stickers may be put on the chest; gel is applied and a probe is moved over the chest to see the heart beating, its valves and blood flow.
It is painless and uses no radiation.
echo.preparation: No special preparation. Children should be calm — bring a favourite toy or feed a baby just before.

procedure: At the branch the patient gives their referral ID at the front desk and pays.
Small metal discs (electrodes) are attached to the scalp with a sticky paste or cap.
The patient rests quietly with eyes closed; they may be asked to breathe deeply and look at flashing lights.
Brain activity is recorded on a computer. It is painless; the paste washes out of the hair.
eeg.preparation: Wash hair the night before — no oils, gels or hair cream. Continue usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise. Some EEGs need the patient to sleep less the night before — the branch will say.

procedure: At the branch the patient gives their referral ID at the front desk and pays.
Everyone being tested brings photo ID (birth certificate or photo for children); identities are recorded and photographs taken for the chain of custody.
A soft swab is rubbed inside each person’s cheek for a few seconds.
The swabs are sealed in front of the participants and sent to the DNA laboratory.
dna.preparation: Do not eat, drink or smoke for 30 minutes before. A parent or legal guardian must consent for children under 18.

procedure: At the branch the patient gives their referral ID at the front desk and pays.
The patient answers questions about their health and medical history.
Height, weight, blood pressure, pulse and vision are checked, and a doctor examines the patient.
Some examinations include basic tests (blood, urine, chest X-ray) depending on the purpose; a report is issued.
medical.preparation: Bring valid ID, any form required by the employer, school or embassy, and previous results. Fasting may be needed if blood tests are included.

procedure: At the branch the patient gives their referral ID at the front desk and pays.
The specialist asks about symptoms and medical history and examines the patient.
Tests such as ECG or echocardiography may be done or requested.
The doctor explains the findings and the treatment plan.
consultation.preparation: Bring previous results, the referral letter and all current medicines.

procedure: The patient (or doctor) asks the branch for a copy of their images.
The images are copied onto a CD or other media.
record.preparation: Bring the receipt or details of the earlier scan.

1: Counts the red cells, white cells and platelets in the blood and measures haemoglobin.
A basic health check used to look for anaemia, infection, inflammation and many other conditions.
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
2: Measures how fast red blood cells settle in a tube — a general sign of inflammation.
Helps detect and follow inflammation, infections and conditions like arthritis.
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
3: Finds the type of haemoglobin a person carries (AA, AS, SS, AC, SC…).
Used to check for sickle cell disease or trait — before marriage, in pregnancy or for a child with symptoms.
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
4: Finds the blood group (A, B, AB or O) and Rhesus factor (positive or negative).
Needed before blood transfusion or surgery, in pregnancy and for records.
5: Counts young red blood cells newly made by the bone marrow.
Shows whether the bone marrow is making enough red cells — used to investigate anaemia.
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
6: A group of tests (PT, INR, PTTK, fibrinogen) that check how well the blood clots.
Done before surgery, for unexplained bleeding or bruising, and to monitor blood-thinning treatment.
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
7: Measures how long a blood sample takes to form a clot.
A simple check of blood clotting before procedures or when bleeding is suspected.
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
8: Measures how long a small skin cut takes to stop bleeding.
Checks how well platelets and small blood vessels work, e.g. for easy bleeding.
9: Measures how long blood plasma takes to clot (PT).
Checks clotting and liver function, and monitors warfarin treatment.
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
10: Partial thromboplastin time with kaolin (APTT) — another measure of clotting speed.
Investigates bleeding disorders such as haemophilia and monitors heparin treatment.
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
11: A standard way of reporting the prothrombin (clotting) time.
Used to monitor patients on warfarin so the dose stays safe.
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
12: Finds the type of haemoglobin a person carries (AA, AS, SS, AC, SC…).
Used to check for sickle cell disease or trait — before marriage, in pregnancy or for a child with symptoms.
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
13: A drop of blood is spread on a slide and the cells are looked at under the microscope.
Shows the shape and look of blood cells — for anaemia, infections, malaria and blood disorders.
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
14: Packed cell volume (haematocrit) — the share of the blood made up of red cells.
A quick check for anaemia or dehydration, often in pregnancy.
15: Counts the platelets — the cells that help blood clot.
Checks for low or high platelets, e.g. in bleeding, bruising, dengue or on some medicines.
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
16: Measures von Willebrand factor, a protein that helps platelets stick and blood clot.
Investigates von Willebrand disease — a common inherited bleeding disorder.
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
17: Coombs tests look for antibodies that attack red blood cells (direct and indirect).
Used in pregnancy (Rhesus negative mothers), before transfusion and when red cells are being destroyed.
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
18: Measures the G6PD enzyme that protects red blood cells.
Checks for G6PD deficiency, which can cause anaemia after some medicines (e.g. some antimalarials), beans or infections.
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
19: Measures fibrinogen, a protein needed to form blood clots.
Investigates bleeding or clotting problems and severe illness.
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
20: Measures C-peptide, made in equal amounts with the body’s own insulin.
Shows how much insulin the pancreas still makes — helps classify diabetes.
Fast for 8–12 hours before the test — no food or drinks except plain water. Coming early in the morning makes fasting easier.
21: A screen for autoantibodies (antibodies against the body’s own tissues).
Investigates autoimmune diseases such as lupus and arthritis.
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
22: Fasting blood sugar — the glucose level after not eating.
Fast for 8–12 hours before the test — no food or drinks except plain water. Coming early in the morning makes fasting easier.
23: Random blood sugar — glucose at any time of day.
A quick check for high or low blood sugar and diabetes.
24: Oral glucose tolerance test — blood sugar is measured before and after drinking a glucose drink.
Diagnoses diabetes and diabetes in pregnancy (gestational diabetes).

Fast for 8–12 hours before (plain water only). The patient stays at the branch for about 2 hours after the glucose drink and should not eat or smoke. Fast for 8–12 hours before the test — no food or drinks except plain water. Coming early in the morning makes fasting easier.
25: Two-hour postprandial sugar — blood sugar 2 hours after a meal.
Shows how well the body handles sugar after eating; used for diabetes.
Eat a normal meal, note the time, and have the blood drawn exactly 2 hours later. No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
26: Electrolytes, urea and creatinine — the main kidney function panel.
Checks kidney function and salt balance; before surgery, CT contrast and many medicines.
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
27: Measures sodium, a key salt in the blood.
Checks fluid and salt balance, e.g. with vomiting, diarrhoea, confusion or on water tablets.
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
28: Measures potassium, important for the heart and muscles.
Checks kidney function and the effect of medicines on salt balance.
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
29: Measures chloride, a salt that works with sodium.
Part of checking fluid, acid and salt balance.
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
30: Measures bicarbonate, which shows the acid balance of the blood.
Checks for acid problems in kidney disease, diabetes or severe illness.
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
31: Measures urea, a waste product removed by the kidneys.
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
32: Measures creatinine, a waste product of muscles cleared by the kidneys.
The main blood test of kidney function.
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
33: A panel of liver enzymes, bilirubin and proteins.
Checks how well the liver works — for jaundice, hepatitis, alcohol use or medicines.
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
34: Measures bilirubin, the yellow pigment from old red cells.
Investigates jaundice (yellow eyes/skin) and liver problems.
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
35: Measures the part of bilirubin already processed by the liver.
Helps find the cause of jaundice (liver or bile ducts).
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
36: ALP — an enzyme from the liver and bones.
Investigates liver, bile duct and bone disease.
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
37: AST (aspartate aminotransferase) — a liver and muscle enzyme.
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
38: ALT (alanine aminotransferase) — the most liver-specific enzyme.
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
39: Gamma-GT — a liver and bile duct enzyme.
Detects bile duct problems and alcohol-related liver injury.
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
40: Measures all the proteins in the blood (albumin and globulins).
Checks nutrition and liver or kidney disease.
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
41: Checks bones, kidneys and the parathyroid glands.
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
42: Measures albumin, the main protein made by the liver.
Checks liver function, nutrition and kidney protein loss; low levels cause swelling.
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
43: Measures uric acid, a waste product from food and cells.
Investigates gout, joint pain and kidney stones.
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
44: BUN — the nitrogen part of urea in the blood.
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
45: Assesses the risk of heart disease and stroke; monitors cholesterol treatment.
Fast for 8–12 hours before the test — no food or drinks except plain water. Coming early in the morning makes fasting easier.
46: Measures all the cholesterol in the blood.
A screen for heart disease risk.
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
47: Measures triglycerides, a type of fat in the blood.
Part of heart risk assessment; very high levels can cause pancreatitis.
Fast for 8–12 hours before the test — no food or drinks except plain water. Coming early in the morning makes fasting easier.
48: “Good” cholesterol that carries cholesterol away from the arteries.
Part of assessing heart disease risk.
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
49: Lactate dehydrogenase — an enzyme released when cells are damaged.
A general marker of tissue damage, haemolysis and some cancers.
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
50: A dipstick and microscope check of the urine (protein, sugar, blood, infection).
A routine screen for kidney disease, diabetes and urinary infection, and in pregnancy.
If possible, give the first urine of the morning. Women should tell staff if they are on their period.
51: Shows the average blood sugar over the last 2–3 months.
Diagnoses diabetes and shows how well it has been controlled.
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
52: Detects active H. pylori infection from the breath.
The most accurate non-invasive test for H. pylori and to confirm cure.
Fast for at least 6 hours. Stop antibiotics 4 weeks and stomach-acid medicines (e.g. omeprazole) 2 weeks before, if the doctor agrees.
53: An antibody often found in rheumatoid arthritis.
Helps diagnose rheumatoid arthritis in people with painful, swollen joints.
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
54: CRP — a protein the liver makes when there is inflammation or infection.
Detects and follows infection and inflammation.
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
55: Detects the pregnancy hormone hCG in urine (or blood).
Confirms pregnancy, e.g. after a missed period or before X-rays.
If possible, give the first urine of the morning. Women should tell staff if they are on their period.
56: A panel of reproductive hormones (FSH, LH, prolactin, oestradiol, progesterone, testosterone).
Investigates infertility, irregular periods and hormone problems.

Women: usually on day 2–3 of the cycle (progesterone around day 21) — the branch or doctor confirms the day. No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
57: Measures progesterone, the hormone that rises after ovulation.
Checks whether ovulation happened (usually tested around day 21) and early pregnancy.
Usually taken about 7 days before the next period (day 21 of a 28-day cycle). No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
58: LH — the hormone that triggers ovulation and testosterone production.
Investigates infertility, irregular periods and menopause.
Women: usually day 2–3 of the cycle. No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
59: FSH — the hormone that makes eggs and sperm mature.
Investigates infertility, irregular periods and menopause.
Women: usually day 2–3 of the cycle. No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
60: Investigates breast milk discharge, irregular periods and infertility.
Best taken in the morning, at rest. No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
61: Investigates periods, fertility, menopause and fertility treatment.
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
62: Measures testosterone, the main male hormone (also present in women).
Investigates low libido, erection problems, infertility and excess hair in women (PCOS).
Best taken in the morning (7–10 am). No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
63: Screens for and monitors prostate problems, including prostate cancer, in men.
Avoid ejaculation and vigorous cycling for 48 hours before. No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
64: Thyroid function tests — TSH with T3 and T4 hormones.
Checks for an overactive or underactive thyroid (weight change, tiredness, palpitations, goitre).
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
65: A tumour marker mainly linked with ovarian cancer.
Investigates ovarian masses and monitors ovarian cancer treatment.
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
66: A tumour marker linked with breast cancer.
Monitors breast cancer treatment and recurrence.
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
67: A tumour marker linked with pancreatic and bile-duct cancers.
Monitors these cancers and investigates pancreatic masses.
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
68: Measures calprotectin, a marker of bowel inflammation.
Helps tell inflammatory bowel disease from irritable bowel syndrome.
Collect the container from the branch first. Tell the lab about any antibiotics or diarrhoea medicine being taken.
69: Mainly used to monitor bowel cancer.
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
70: A form of the enzyme creatine kinase found mainly in heart muscle.
Helps detect heart muscle damage (heart attack).
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
71: Measures cortisol, the stress hormone from the adrenal glands.
Taken in the morning (around 8–9 am). No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
72: CRP — a protein the liver makes when there is inflammation or infection.
Detects and follows infection and inflammation.
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
73: High-sensitivity CRP — detects low levels of inflammation.
Adds to heart disease risk assessment.
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
74: Measures cystatin C, a protein cleared by the kidneys.
A sensitive check of kidney function, useful when creatinine is unreliable.
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
75: Measures a fragment released when a blood clot breaks down.
Helps rule out a blood clot in the leg (DVT) or lungs (pulmonary embolism).
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
76: AFP — a protein made by the liver and the unborn baby.
A marker for liver cancer and some testicular tumours; also used in pregnancy screening.
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
77: Ferritin — the protein that stores iron in the body.
The best single test of the body’s iron stores, for anaemia or iron overload.
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
78: Faecal occult blood — finds hidden blood in the stool.
Screens for bleeding in the gut, polyps and bowel cancer.
Collect the container from the branch first. Tell the lab about any antibiotics or diarrhoea medicine being taken.
79: Measures the pregnancy hormone hCG in the blood (quantitative).
Confirms and follows early pregnancy; checks for ectopic pregnancy or miscarriage.
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
80: Measures the insulin hormone in the blood.
Investigates low blood sugar, insulin resistance and some types of diabetes.
Fast for 8–12 hours before the test — no food or drinks except plain water. Coming early in the morning makes fasting easier.
81: Total immunoglobulin E — the antibody involved in allergy.
Investigates allergies, asthma, eczema and some parasite infections.
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
82: Detects tiny amounts of albumin protein in the urine.
Early sign of kidney damage in diabetes and high blood pressure.
If possible, give the first urine of the morning. Women should tell staff if they are on their period.
83: Myoglobin — a protein released from damaged muscle.
Detects muscle injury and early heart muscle damage.
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
84: A marker that rises mainly in bacterial infection.
Helps tell bacterial from viral infection and guides antibiotics in severe illness.
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
85: Troponin I — a protein released when heart muscle is damaged.
The key blood test for a heart attack in someone with chest pain.
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
86: Troponin T — a protein released when heart muscle is damaged.
Used to detect a heart attack and heart strain.
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
87: Stool microscopy, culture and sensitivity — looks for bacteria, parasites and worms.
Investigates diarrhoea, dysentery, typhoid and worm infections.
Collect the container from the branch first. Tell the lab about any antibiotics or diarrhoea medicine being taken.
88: Blood is incubated to grow any bacteria or fungi, then tested against antibiotics.
Finds the cause of serious infections and fevers (e.g. typhoid, sepsis).
Ideally taken before starting antibiotics. No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
89: Urine microscopy, culture and sensitivity — grows any germs and finds the right antibiotic.
Confirms a urinary tract infection and guides antibiotic choice.
If possible, give the first urine of the morning. Women should tell staff if they are on their period.
90: A swab from the affected area is cultured to grow germs.
Finds the cause of an infection and the right antibiotic.
If possible, come before starting antibiotics. For a throat swab, don’t eat or drink for 30 minutes before.
91: Finds the germ causing a chest infection and the right antibiotic.
Collect the container from the branch first. The early-morning sample is the best one.
92: Acid-fast bacilli smear on three sputum samples.
Detects tuberculosis germs in people with a long-lasting cough.
Three early-morning sputum samples on 3 different days. Collect the container from the branch first. The early-morning sample is the best one.
93: Malaria parasite test — looks for malaria in the blood (slide or rapid test).
Diagnoses malaria in someone with fever, chills or headache.
94: Looks for antibodies to typhoid bacteria.
A screening test for typhoid fever (a blood or stool culture confirms it).
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
95: Cells from the cervix are checked for abnormal changes.
Screens for cervical cancer and pre-cancer changes.
Best done mid-cycle, not during a period. Avoid sex, douching and vaginal creams for 48 hours before.
96: Screens for HIV-1 and HIV-2 infection.
Routine screening, in pregnancy, before surgery or after a possible exposure.
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
97: Investigates jaundice and acute liver infection.
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
98: Hepatitis B surface antigen — shows hepatitis B infection.
Screens for hepatitis B (routine, pregnancy, before surgery or vaccination).
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
99: No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
100: Routine screening, in pregnancy and for sexually transmitted infections.
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
101: A panel of hepatitis B markers (HBsAg, HBeAg and antibodies).
Shows whether hepatitis B is active, past or vaccinated against.
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
102: Tests on spinal fluid — cells, sugar, protein and germs.
Diagnoses meningitis and other brain or nerve conditions.
Arranged by the patient’s doctor or hospital — the branch receives and tests the sample.
103: Tests for Helicobacter pylori, the germ that causes stomach ulcers.
Investigates ulcers, indigestion and upper tummy pain.
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
104: Faecal occult blood — finds hidden blood in the stool.
Screens for bleeding in the gut, polyps and bowel cancer.
Collect the container from the branch first. Tell the lab about any antibiotics or diarrhoea medicine being taken.
105: Urine is looked at under the microscope for cells, crystals and germs.
Investigates urinary infection, kidney disease and blood in urine.
If possible, give the first urine of the morning. Women should tell staff if they are on their period.
106: Stool is looked at under the microscope for parasites, eggs and blood cells.
Detects worms and parasites causing tummy pain or diarrhoea.
Collect the container from the branch first. Tell the lab about any antibiotics or diarrhoea medicine being taken.
107: Antibodies to H. pylori in the blood.
Shows current or past H. pylori infection in people with ulcers or indigestion.
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
108: An antibody often found in rheumatoid arthritis.
Helps diagnose rheumatoid arthritis in people with painful, swollen joints.
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
109: A quick microscope stain that groups bacteria.
Gives an early clue to the germ causing an infection.
If possible, come before starting antibiotics. For a throat swab, don’t eat or drink for 30 minutes before.
110: Anti-streptolysin O — antibodies after a strep throat infection.
Investigates rheumatic fever, joint pain and kidney problems after a sore throat.
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
111: Investigates chlamydia infection, pelvic infection and blocked tubes in infertility.
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
112: Looks for filarial worm larvae in the blood.
Investigates filariasis (elephantiasis, swollen legs, itchy skin).
Some types are best detected in blood taken at night — the branch advises. No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
113: A panel of hepatitis B markers (HBsAg, HBeAg and antibodies).
Shows whether hepatitis B is active, past or vaccinated against.
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
114: Antibodies to Toxoplasma, Rubella, CMV and Herpes.
Checks for infections that can harm an unborn baby — in pregnancy or after miscarriage.
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
115: Checks immunity before or during pregnancy and recent infection.
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
116: Checks for infection in pregnancy that could affect the baby.
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
117: Antibodies to herpes simplex viruses 1 and 2.
Shows recent or past herpes infection (cold sores, genital sores).
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
118: Sperm analysis plus a culture for infection.
Assesses male fertility and looks for infection affecting sperm.
No ejaculation for 2–5 days before the test (but not more than 7). Avoid alcohol for a few days. Do not use lubricants or condoms to collect the sample.
119: Checks sperm count, movement and shape.
Assesses male fertility and checks vasectomy results.
No ejaculation for 2–5 days before the test (but not more than 7). Avoid alcohol for a few days. Do not use lubricants or condoms to collect the sample.
120: Measures HIV in the blood and tests which medicines it resists.
Guides HIV treatment when it is not working.
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
121: Measures the amount of hepatitis B virus in the blood.
Decides on and monitors hepatitis B treatment.
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
122: Identifies the type (genotype) of hepatitis C virus.
Guides the choice and length of hepatitis C treatment.
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
123: Antinuclear antibodies — a screen for autoimmune disease.
Helps diagnose lupus and other connective-tissue diseases.
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
124: Investigates vasculitis (inflamed blood vessels) affecting kidneys, lungs or sinuses.
No special preparation. The patient should take usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise.
125: Ultrasound of the bladder and pelvic organs (womb and ovaries in women).
Investigates pelvic pain, period problems, fibroids and ovarian cysts.
Come with a full bladder: drink 4–6 glasses (about 1 litre) of water an hour before and do not urinate until after the scan.
126: Ultrasound of the abdomen and pelvis — liver, gallbladder, kidneys, spleen, bladder and pelvic organs.
Investigates tummy pain, swelling, gallstones, kidney problems and pelvic masses.
No food for 6–8 hours before (plain water is fine), so the gallbladder and organs show clearly. For the pelvic part, drink 4–6 glasses of water an hour before and don’t empty the bladder.
127: Pregnancy ultrasound of the baby, placenta and fluid.
Checks the baby’s growth, position, heartbeat and the due date.

In early pregnancy come with a full bladder; later in pregnancy no preparation is needed. Come with a full bladder: drink 4–6 glasses (about 1 litre) of water an hour before and do not urinate until after the scan.
128: Ultrasound of the thyroid gland in the neck.
No special preparation. Wear loose, comfortable clothing.
129: Investigates breast lumps, pain and discharge — especially in younger women.
No special preparation. Wear loose, comfortable clothing.
130: Ultrasound of the testicles, scrotum and prostate.
Investigates swelling, pain, lumps and urinary problems in men.
No special preparation. Wear loose, comfortable clothing.
131: Doppler ultrasound of the blood vessels in both legs (or arms).
Looks for blood clots (DVT), narrowed arteries and varicose veins.
No special preparation. Wear loose clothing.
132: Doppler ultrasound of blood flow in the brain arteries through the skull.
Screens children with sickle cell for stroke risk; checks brain blood flow.
No special preparation. Wear loose clothing.
133: Investigates testicular pain, swelling, lumps and infertility.
No special preparation. Wear loose, comfortable clothing.
134: Ultrasound of the kidneys and bladder.
Investigates kidney stones, infections, swelling and kidney disease.
Come with a full bladder: drink 4–6 glasses (about 1 litre) of water an hour before and do not urinate until after the scan.
135: A detailed pregnancy scan at about 18–22 weeks.
Checks the baby’s organs and body for abnormalities.
No special preparation. Wear loose, comfortable clothing.
136: Gives a detailed view of the prostate, e.g. with a raised PSA.
An enema or bowel emptying may be asked for before the scan; the branch gives instructions. A partly full bladder may be needed.
137: Ultrasound of the urethra while it is filled with fluid.
Measures narrowing (stricture) of the urethra in men.
No special preparation. Wear loose, comfortable clothing.
138: Ultrasound of a baby’s brain through the soft spot on the head.
Checks newborns and infants for bleeding, fluid build-up (hydrocephalus) and brain problems.
Feed the baby shortly before so they are calm or asleep. Only possible while the soft spot is still open (usually under 12–18 months).
139: A series of scans (3 visits) that follow egg follicles growing in the ovary.
Times ovulation for natural conception or fertility treatment.
Empty the bladder just before the scan. It can be done during a period.
140: Internal ultrasound of the womb and ovaries.
Gives the clearest view for fibroids, cysts, early pregnancy and fertility.
Empty the bladder just before the scan. It can be done during a period.
141: Ultrasound of the neck — glands, thyroid and lumps.
Investigates neck lumps and swollen glands.
No special preparation. Wear loose, comfortable clothing.
142: Ultrasound of a lump or swelling under the skin.
Investigates lumps, abscesses, cysts and swellings.
No special preparation. Wear loose, comfortable clothing.
143: Ultrasound of small structures (thyroid, testes, glands, small lumps).
Investigates small lumps and superficial organs.
No special preparation. Wear loose, comfortable clothing.
144: Doppler ultrasound of blood flow in the penis, after an injection that causes an erection.
Investigates erectile dysfunction and Peyronie’s disease.
No special preparation. Wear loose clothing.
145: An X-ray picture of the hand.
Checks for fractures, dislocations, arthritis and swelling in the hand.
No special preparation. Remove metal items around the area. Tell staff if the patient is or may be pregnant.
146: An X-ray picture of the wrist.
Checks for wrist fractures after a fall and for arthritis.
No special preparation. Remove metal items around the area. Tell staff if the patient is or may be pregnant.
147: An X-ray picture of the forearm (radius and ulna).
Checks for forearm fractures after injury.
No special preparation. Remove metal items around the area. Tell staff if the patient is or may be pregnant.
148: An X-ray picture of the upper arm bone (humerus).
Checks the upper arm for fractures and bone problems.
No special preparation. Remove metal items around the area. Tell staff if the patient is or may be pregnant.
149: An X-ray picture of the shoulder.
Checks for shoulder fractures, dislocation and arthritis.
No special preparation. Remove metal items around the area. Tell staff if the patient is or may be pregnant.
150: An X-ray picture of the shoulder blade (scapula).
Checks the shoulder blade after a fall or blow.
No special preparation. Remove metal items around the area. Tell staff if the patient is or may be pregnant.
151: An X-ray picture of the foot.
Checks the foot for fractures, heel spurs and arthritis.
No special preparation. Remove metal items around the area. Tell staff if the patient is or may be pregnant.
152: An X-ray picture of the lower leg (tibia and fibula).
Checks the shin bones for fractures after injury.
No special preparation. Remove metal items around the area. Tell staff if the patient is or may be pregnant.
153: An X-ray picture of the thigh bone (femur).
Checks the thigh bone for fractures and bone problems.
No special preparation. Remove metal items around the area. Tell staff if the patient is or may be pregnant.
154: An X-ray picture of the pelvis.
Checks the pelvis and hip joints after a fall and for arthritis.
No special preparation. Remove metal items around the area. Tell staff if the patient is or may be pregnant.
155: An X-ray picture of the both hip joints.
Investigates hip pain, arthritis and hip problems in children.
No special preparation. Remove metal items around the area. Tell staff if the patient is or may be pregnant.
156: An X-ray picture of the chest (front view).
Looks at the lungs, heart and chest — for cough, chest infection, TB and breathlessness; often for work or travel medicals.
No special preparation. Remove metal items around the area. Tell staff if the patient is or may be pregnant.
157: An X-ray picture of the chest (front and side views).
A fuller view of the lungs, heart and chest when a single view isn’t enough.
No special preparation. Remove metal items around the area. Tell staff if the patient is or may be pregnant.
158: An X-ray picture of the skull.
Checks the skull bones after a head injury and for bone problems.
No special preparation. Remove metal items around the area. Tell staff if the patient is or may be pregnant.
159: An X-ray picture of the sinuses.
Investigates sinusitis, facial pain and blocked nose.
No special preparation. Remove metal items around the area. Tell staff if the patient is or may be pregnant.
160: An X-ray picture of the jaw (mandible).
Checks for jaw fractures, dental problems and jaw joint pain.
No special preparation. Remove metal items around the area. Tell staff if the patient is or may be pregnant.
161: Screens for breast cancer and investigates breast lumps, pain or nipple discharge (usually from age 40).
Do not use deodorant, talcum powder or lotion under the arms or on the breasts on the day. Best done the week after a period, when breasts are less tender.
162: An X-ray picture of the nasopharynx (back of the nose).
Checks for enlarged adenoids in children who snore or breathe through the mouth.
No special preparation. Remove metal items around the area. Tell staff if the patient is or may be pregnant.
163: An X-ray picture of the upper and middle back (thoracic spine).
Investigates upper back pain, injury and curvature.
No special preparation. Remove metal items around the area. Tell staff if the patient is or may be pregnant.
164: An X-ray picture of the lower back (lumbosacral spine).
Investigates low back pain, injury and spine wear.
No special preparation. Remove metal items around the area. Tell staff if the patient is or may be pregnant.
165: An X-ray picture of the knee.
Investigates knee pain, swelling, injury and arthritis.
No special preparation. Remove metal items around the area. Tell staff if the patient is or may be pregnant.
166: An X-ray picture of the neck (cervical spine).
Investigates neck pain, injury and spine wear (spondylosis).
No special preparation. Remove metal items around the area. Tell staff if the patient is or may be pregnant.
167: An X-ray picture of the thoracic inlet (base of the neck and top of the chest).
Checks for a goitre pressing on the windpipe and other masses at the base of the neck.
No special preparation. Remove metal items around the area. Tell staff if the patient is or may be pregnant.
168: Loopogram — X-ray of a bowel or bladder loop (stoma) with dye.
Checks a stoma or urinary conduit after surgery.
The branch gives specific instructions when booking. Tell staff about allergies to contrast dye and about pregnancy.
169: An X-ray picture of the post-nasal space (behind the nose).
Looks for enlarged adenoids or masses behind the nose.
No special preparation. Remove metal items around the area. Tell staff if the patient is or may be pregnant.
170: An X-ray picture of the abdomen.
Looks for bowel blockage, swallowed objects and some stones.
No special preparation. Remove metal items around the area. Tell staff if the patient is or may be pregnant.
171: An X-ray picture of the whole skeleton.
A series of X-rays of the bones — for myeloma, bone spread of cancer, or suspected injuries in children.
No special preparation. Remove metal items around the area. Tell staff if the patient is or may be pregnant.
172: An X-ray picture of the pituitary fossa (the bony pocket holding the pituitary gland).
Looks for enlargement of the pituitary area.
No special preparation. Remove metal items around the area. Tell staff if the patient is or may be pregnant.
173: An X-ray picture of the mastoid bones behind the ears.
Investigates mastoiditis and chronic ear infections.
No special preparation. Remove metal items around the area. Tell staff if the patient is or may be pregnant.
174: X-ray of the gullet (oesophagus) while swallowing barium.
Investigates difficulty or pain swallowing and reflux.
Usually no food or drink for 6 hours before. A barium enema needs bowel preparation (laxatives) the day before — the branch gives the instructions.
175: X-ray pictures as barium travels through the small bowel.
Investigates the small intestine — pain, diarrhoea, Crohn’s disease.
Usually no food or drink for 6 hours before. A barium enema needs bowel preparation (laxatives) the day before — the branch gives the instructions.
176: X-ray of the stomach and first part of the bowel after drinking barium.
Investigates ulcers, indigestion and stomach problems.
Usually no food or drink for 6 hours before. A barium enema needs bowel preparation (laxatives) the day before — the branch gives the instructions.
177: X-ray of the large bowel filled with barium through the back passage.
Investigates bowel habit change, bleeding and colon problems.

Bowel preparation with laxatives is needed the day before. Usually no food or drink for 6 hours before. A barium enema needs bowel preparation (laxatives) the day before — the branch gives the instructions.
178: Hysterosalpingogram — X-ray of the womb and fallopian tubes with dye.
Checks whether the fallopian tubes are open in women trying to conceive.
Booked between day 7 and day 10 of the cycle (after the period ends, before ovulation). Avoid unprotected sex from the period until the test. A painkiller 30–60 minutes before can help.
179: Retrograde cystourethrogram — X-ray of the urethra and bladder with dye.
Investigates narrowing (stricture) of the urethra in men.
The branch gives specific instructions when booking. Tell staff about allergies to contrast dye and about pregnancy.
180: Micturating cystourethrogram — X-ray while the bladder empties.
Checks for urine flowing back to the kidneys (reflux), often in children with infections.
The branch gives specific instructions when booking. Tell staff about allergies to contrast dye and about pregnancy.
181: X-ray of an abnormal channel (fistula) filled with dye.
Shows where a fistula or sinus track goes before treatment.
The branch gives specific instructions when booking. Tell staff about allergies to contrast dye and about pregnancy.
182: Electroencephalogram — a recording of the brain’s electrical activity.
Investigates seizures/epilepsy, fainting spells and some sleep or behaviour problems.
Wash hair the night before — no oils, gels or hair cream. Continue usual medicines unless the doctor says otherwise. Some EEGs need the patient to sleep less the night before — the branch will say.
183: An ultrasound scan of the heart for babies and children.
Checks for heart defects (holes in the heart) and murmurs in children.
No special preparation. Children should be calm — bring a favourite toy or feed a baby just before.
184: An ultrasound scan of the heart (adults).
Shows the heart’s pumping strength, valves and walls — for breathlessness, murmurs, heart failure and high blood pressure.
No special preparation. Children should be calm — bring a favourite toy or feed a baby just before.
185: Electrocardiogram — a recording of the heart’s electrical activity.
Checks heart rhythm and signs of heart attack or strain — for chest pain, palpitations, high blood pressure and pre-surgery checks.
Avoid body lotion or oil on the chest on the day. Wear a top that is easy to remove. Bring a list of medicines.
186: A 24-hour ECG recording with a small portable recorder.
Catches irregular heartbeats that come and go — palpitations, dizziness or fainting.
Have a bath or shower before coming — the recorder must not get wet. Wear loose clothing. Avoid electric blankets and keep phones a little away from the recorder.
187: A camera examination of the whole large bowel.
Investigates bleeding from the back passage, bowel habit change, anaemia and screens for bowel cancer.
The bowel must be empty: a low-fibre diet for 2 days, clear fluids only the day before and a bowel-cleansing laxative as instructed by the branch. If sedated, someone must accompany the patient home.
188: A camera examination of the gullet, stomach and first part of the bowel.
Investigates ulcers, persistent indigestion, vomiting blood and anaemia.
No food for 6–8 hours and no drinks for 2–4 hours before. If sedated, someone must accompany the patient home.
189: A camera examination of the throat and voice box.
Investigates hoarseness, throat pain, difficulty swallowing and lumps in the throat.
Usually avoid eating for 2 hours before; the branch confirms.
190: A camera examination of the gullet (oesophagus).
Investigates difficulty swallowing, reflux and bleeding.
No food for 6–8 hours and no drinks for 2–4 hours before. If sedated, someone must accompany the patient home.
191: A general medical examination by a doctor.
For employment, school, travel or fitness certificates and general health checks.
Bring valid ID, any form required by the employer, school or embassy, and previous results. Fasting may be needed if blood tests are included.
192: A CT scan of the head and brain.
Quick assessment after head injury, stroke, sudden severe headache or confusion.
Remove metal items. Tell staff if the patient is or may be pregnant.
193: A CT of the brain and the neck bones.
After accidents or falls with head and neck injury.
Remove metal items. Tell staff if the patient is or may be pregnant.
194: A CT of the abdomen with contrast dye.
Tummy pain, appendicitis, masses, liver and pancreas problems.

No food for 4–6 hours before (water is fine). Tell staff about allergies to contrast or iodine, kidney disease, diabetes medicine (metformin) and pregnancy. A recent kidney test (E/U/C) may be requested.
195: A CT of the abdomen and pelvis with contrast dye.
Tummy and pelvic pain, masses and bowel problems.

No food for 4–6 hours before (water is fine). Tell staff about allergies to contrast or iodine, kidney disease, diabetes medicine (metformin) and pregnancy. A recent kidney test (E/U/C) may be requested.
196: A CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis together.
Staging and following up cancers; finding the source of illness.

No food for 4–6 hours before (water is fine). Tell staff about allergies to contrast or iodine, kidney disease, diabetes medicine (metformin) and pregnancy. A recent kidney test (E/U/C) may be requested.
197: A CT of the kidneys, ureters and bladder with contrast.
Blood in the urine, kidney stones and urinary tract masses.

No food for 4–6 hours before (water is fine). Tell staff about allergies to contrast or iodine, kidney disease, diabetes medicine (metformin) and pregnancy. A recent kidney test (E/U/C) may be requested.
198: A CT of the chest with contrast dye.
Lung masses, blood clots in the lungs, chest infections and staging cancer.

No food for 4–6 hours before (water is fine). Tell staff about allergies to contrast or iodine, kidney disease, diabetes medicine (metformin) and pregnancy. A recent kidney test (E/U/C) may be requested.
199: Chronic sinusitis and planning sinus surgery.
Remove metal items. Tell staff if the patient is or may be pregnant.
200: A CT of the upper and middle back.
Spine fractures and bone problems in the thoracic spine.
Remove metal items. Tell staff if the patient is or may be pregnant.
201: Neck lumps, throat and voice-box masses, and spread of cancer.

No food for 4–6 hours before (water is fine). Tell staff about allergies to contrast or iodine, kidney disease, diabetes medicine (metformin) and pregnancy. A recent kidney test (E/U/C) may be requested.
202: A CT of the lower back.
Lower spine fractures, slipped discs and bone problems.
Remove metal items. Tell staff if the patient is or may be pregnant.
203: A tissue sample taken with a needle guided by CT.
Safely samples deep lumps (lung, liver, bone) for diagnosis.
Stop blood thinners as advised by the doctor; a clotting test may be needed. Someone should accompany the patient home. Remove metal items. Tell staff if the patient is or may be pregnant.
204: A CT of the middle and lower back.
Spine injuries and bone problems across the back.
Remove metal items. Tell staff if the patient is or may be pregnant.
205: A CT of the skull and facial bones.
Facial fractures, sinus and skull problems; planning surgery.
Remove metal items. Tell staff if the patient is or may be pregnant.
206: A CT of the thigh bone.
Complex thigh-bone fractures and bone lesions.
Remove metal items. Tell staff if the patient is or may be pregnant.
207: Complex knee fractures and planning surgery.
Remove metal items. Tell staff if the patient is or may be pregnant.
208: A liver CT taken at three moments as contrast flows through.
